html:
The actor–critic decomposition introduced in the loss-function section is best treated, at the level of anatomy, as a biased architectural motif rather than a literal two-box partition. In the clean RL formalism, the critic estimates value and helps generate the teaching signal, whereas the actor converts that teaching signal into policy updates. The basal ganglia appear to implement something close to this logic, but they do so through partially overlapping gradients, loops, and compartments rather than through one anatomically isolated “critic nucleus” and one isolated “actor nucleus” 1, 2, 3. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

At the coarsest scale, the most important organizing principle is a ventromedial-to-dorsolateral gradient across striatum. As one moves from nucleus accumbens and ventromedial striatum toward dorsomedial and then dorsolateral striatum, neural coding shifts from relatively stronger value, expectation, and motivational variables toward relatively stronger action, associative, and sensorimotor variables. This gradient is exactly what one would expect from an approximate actor–critic architecture: ventral territories are more critic-like because they are more strongly concerned with state and motivational value, whereas dorsal territories are more actor-like because they are more tightly linked to action selection, action chunks, and habit-like control 3, 4, 5, 6. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The ventral striatum is especially well placed to implement the critic side of the architecture. The classical reason is computational: it has access to phasic dopaminergic prediction-error signals and receives convergent limbic, hippocampal, orbitofrontal, medial prefrontal, and thalamic information appropriate for computing state value and expected utility. But the anatomical reason is at least as important: ventral striatum sits in a strategic position to influence the very dopaminergic teaching signals on which both critic and actor depend, via its projections through ventral pallidum and related ventral midbrain circuitry. As van der Meer and Redish emphasized, ventral striatum has unusually good access to prediction-error inputs; and as earlier actor–critic interpretations stressed, it is in a prime position to shape prediction-error learning signals for both systems, not merely to receive them 2, 7. More recent projection-specific tracing is broadly consistent with this emphasis: for many dopamine subpopulations, ventral striatum is among the densest input sources, making it a plausible major supplier of critic-like expectation information to the midbrain 8.

The dorsal striatum, by contrast, is better viewed as the actor side of the architecture, though again only in a dominant and not exclusive sense. Recordings in dorsal striatum have repeatedly found action-specific value signals, chosen-action signals, contralateral choice signals, and other variables suitable for policy updating rather than pure state evaluation 4, 9. This is especially clear in dorsomedial striatum for flexible, goal-directed action selection, and in dorsolateral striatum for more sensorimotor and habitual control. Projection-specific dopamine measurements sharpen the point: dopamine terminals in ventral striatum respond more strongly to reward consumption and reward-predicting cues, whereas dorsomedial terminals more strongly encode contralateral choice; yet both still carry RPE-like information 5. Thus the actor is not error-free or critic-free; rather, it is an action-centered substrate trained by regionally tailored error signals 4, 5, 9, 10. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

But how does the critic train the actor? The classical answer is the striato–nigro–striatal spiral. In primates, Haber and colleagues described an ascending spiral in which ventral striatal territories influence progressively more dorsal dopamine-recipient territories through ventral-to-dorsal striatonigral and nigrostriatal connectivity, providing an appealing route by which value learning in ventral loops could progressively tutor action learning in dorsal loops 11. But this should not be stated as though it were the sole or even a fully established mechanism. More recent circuit dissection finds strong evidence for closed loops, which would allow a striatal subregion to regulate its own dopamine release, alongside evidence for open loops that could support cross-region transfer. Likewise, whole-brain tracing of projection-defined dopamine subpopulations suggests that most dopamine groups receive a fairly common set of inputs rather than being organized as neatly closed, target-by-target reciprocal loops; the major outlier is the posterior/tail striatal system, which receives relatively little ventral-striatal input and more pallidal, subthalamic, and zona incerta drive 12, 8. The safest synthesis, then, is that dorsal striatum receives value-relevant information from ventral systems indirectly–through shared dopaminergic broadcasts, ventral-striatal influence on midbrain teaching signals, and open striato–nigro–striatal loops–rather than through a simple monosynaptic “ventral critic to dorsal actor” line.

A second, and in some ways deeper, candidate implementation of the actor–critic architecture lies in the patch/striosome versus matrix organization of the striatum. This mapping is attractive because it places the critic-like function not simply in ventral striatum as a whole, but in those striatal compartments that are anatomically specialized to control dopamine neurons directly. Striosomal neurons form the unusual striosome–dendron bouquet arrangements that target dopamine-containing dendrites and clustered nigral cell bodies, strongly suggesting a specialized route by which striatum can regulate the computation and routing of dopaminergic teaching signals 13. Lazaridis and colleagues then showed that striosomes contain parallel D1- and D2-defined pathways that target dopamine neurons rather than the canonical basal-ganglia motor output nuclei, with net effects opposite to the standard direct/indirect pathways (i.e S-D1 is net inhibitory and S-D2 is net excitatory); and Cai and colleagues showed that patch activation suppresses locomotion and strongly inhibits dopamine release, whereas matrix striatonigral activation promotes locomotion and initially promotes dopamine release 14, 15. On this view, the matrix is naturally actor-like because it is more tightly embedded in the canonical action-output channels, whereas striosomes are naturally critic-like because they are disproportionately positioned to compute, gate, and sculpt the dopaminergic teaching signal that trains those channels.

The compartment story also clarifies why the actor–critic mapping should remain graded rather than absolute. Striosomes are not pure critics, matrix is not pure actor 16, ventral striatum can participate in performance and incentive invigoration, and dorsal striatum still carries value signals. Even at the local physiological level, dopamine affects striosome and matrix neurons differently rather than simply exciting one and ignoring the other: dopamine can prolong up-states in matrix D1 neurons while shortening them in striosomal D1 neurons, implying that the microarchitecture is built for differential learning rules, not for a single uniform policy substrate 17. The right conclusion is therefore not that the BG literally contain one critic and one actor, but that they contain nested actor–critic-like motifs: a ventral-to-dorsal territorial gradient, a striosome-to-matrix compartmental specialization, and a projection-specific dopamine system that broadcasts partly shared but regionally customized teaching signals. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

In that sense, the potential architectural underpinnings of the dorsal/ventral actor–critic subdivision are now clearer. The critic-like side of the system is implemented by circuits that estimate motivational/state value and that can reach back to the dopamine system—most prominently ventral striatum, ventral pallidum, and striosomal pathways to midbrain dopamine neurons. The actor-like side is implemented by circuits more directly coupled to action competition and policy expression—especially matrix-rich dorsal striatal loops projecting through the canonical basal-ganglia output channels. Dopamine links the two: it is the shared teaching signal, but it is not perfectly homogeneous. Rather, it is routed through topographically organized, partially looping, and compartmentally gated architectures that allow critic-like valuation to train actor-like policy at multiple anatomical scales 18, 5, 6.
